slides.content:
Root Causes of the War
- Slavery: 4 million enslaved African Americans in the South
- States' Rights: Southern states asserted the right to nullify federal law
- Economic Divide: Tariffs favored Northern industry, hurt Southern agriculture
- Territorial Expansion: Fierce debate over slavery in new western territories
- Bleeding Kansas & the breakdown of political compromise

The War Begins (1861)
- April 12, 1861: Confederate forces fire on Fort Sumter, South Carolina — war begins
- 11 Southern states form the Confederate States of America
- First Battle of Bull Run (July 1861): Shock victory for the Confederacy
- Both sides expected a short war — they were wrong
- Union strategy: Anaconda Plan — blockade Southern ports, control the Mississippi River

Major Battles
- Battle of Antietam (Sept 1862): Bloodiest single day — 22,000 casualties
- Battle of Gettysburg (July 1–3, 1863): Turning point; 51,000 total casualties
- Siege of Vicksburg (1863): Union gains control of the Mississippi River
- Sherman's March to the Sea (1864): Total war strategy devastates the South
- Appomattox Court House (April 9, 1865): Lee surrenders to Grant — war ends

slides.content:
The Emancipation Proclamation
- Issued by President Lincoln on January 1, 1863
- Declared all enslaved people in Confederate states 'forever free'
- Reframed the war: from preserving the Union to ending slavery
- 180,000 Black soldiers joined the Union Army (United States Colored Troops)
- Paved the way for the 13th Amendment (1865): Abolition of slavery nationwide

Union deaths: ~360,000
Confederate deaths: ~260,000
Civilian casualties: ~50,000+
Total cost: ~$6.2 billion (1860s dollars)
Duration: 4 years, 3 weeks, 6 days
Battles fought: Over 10,000 engagements

slides.content:
Reconstruction Era (1865–1877)
- Rebuilding the South and reintegrating Confederate states
- 13th, 14th & 15th Amendments: Abolition, citizenship, and Black voting rights
- Freedmen's Bureau: Assisted formerly enslaved people with education and employment
- Resistance: Rise of the Ku Klux Klan, Black Codes, and systemic oppression
- Lincoln assassinated April 14, 1865 — a devastating blow to moderate Reconstruction

slides.content:
Legacy & Impact
- Ended slavery and transformed American democracy
- Federal government supremacy over states firmly established
- Industrialization accelerated in the post-war United States
- The war's memory: Lost Cause mythology vs. historical truth
- Foundation of civil rights struggles: from 1865 to the Civil Rights Movement of the 1960s
- The Civil War remains the defining moment of American national identity
